content: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a chronic medical condition with a well-defined clinical profile, though its exact cause remains unknown. It is primarily characterized by persistent, widespread pain and is frequently accompanied by sleep disturbances, cognitive impairments, and fatigue. Patients with FM often experience significant levels of disability and report negative mood states. Psychotherapeutic interventions, such as cognitive behavioral therapies (CBTs), aim to alleviate core symptoms, enhance daily functioning, improve mood, and foster a sense of personal control over pain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and potential adverse effects of CBTs in the treatment of FM, both at the conclusion of therapy and during long-term follow-up (defined as at least six months post-treatment). To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and SCOPUS, up to August 28, 2013. Additional searches were performed on clinical trial registries, such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), to identify ongoing studies. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children, adolescents, or adults diagnosed with FM who underwent CBT interventions. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were conducted independently by two reviewers, with any disagreements resolved through discussion. A total of 23 studies, encompassing 24 CBT intervention arms, were included in the analysis. These studies involved 2,031 participants, with 1,073 individuals assigned to CBT groups and 958 to control groups. Only two studies were deemed to have no risk of bias, and the overall quality of evidence, as assessed using the GRADE framework, was determined to be low. CBTs demonstrated superiority over control interventions in reducing pain, negative mood, and disability. At the end of treatment, pain was reduced by 0.5 points on a 0-to-10 scale (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.29; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.49 to -0.17), and this effect persisted at long-term follow-up (median six months), with a reduction of 0.6 points (SMD -0.40; 95% CI -0.62 to -0.17). Negative mood improved by 0.7 points at the end of treatment (SMD -0.33; 95% CI -0.49 to -0.17) and by 1.3 points at long-term follow-up (SMD -0.43; 95% CI -0.75 to -0.11). Disability scores decreased by 0.7 points at the end of treatment (SMD -0.30; 95% CI -0.51 to -0.08) and by 1.2 points at long-term follow-up (SMD -0.52; 95% CI -0.86 to -0.18). Importantly, there was no statistically significant difference in dropout rates between the CBT and control groups for any reason (risk ratio [RR] 0.94; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.35). In conclusion, CBTs provided modest but statistically significant improvements in pain, negative mood, and disability in individuals with FM, both at the end of treatment and during long-term follow-up. The dropout rates were comparable between CBT and control groups, suggesting that CBTs are a tolerable intervention for this patient population.
